The NDT Technician Workforce Shortage: What Actually Helps

The NDT industry faces a projected 15% workforce shortage by 2028, driven by an aging workforce and an insufficient pipeline of new entrants — not automation. Here's the honest picture of what actually helps.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · August 10, 2026

The Numbers Behind the Shortage

The scale of the problem is well documented rather than speculative. There are an estimated 500,000+ certified NDT technicians working globally, and the industry faces a projected 15% workforce shortage by 2028. The average NDT technician age is 45, and only about 8% of the workforce is female — both indicators of a pipeline problem more than a demand problem, since NDT industry activity is growing at roughly 8.1% annually. The average time to fill an NDT Level II position has stretched from about 30 days to 45+ days over the past five years, a direct signal of how tight the supply side has gotten. See our full breakdown on the NDT industry statistics page for the complete data set.

What's Actually Driving It

The shortage isn't a mystery, and it isn't a story about technology eliminating jobs — it's a demographic and pipeline problem. An aging workforce (average age 45) means a large cohort is approaching retirement over the coming years. At the same time, the number of new entrants coming into NDT certification hasn't kept pace with both replacement demand and the industry's underlying growth. Low awareness of NDT as a career path, combined with the multi-year experience-hour requirements built into SNT-TC-1A certification (210–1,200 hours at Level I depending on method, more at Level II), means the pipeline takes real time to refill even when new entrants start today.

Why "AI Will Just Replace These Jobs" Misreads the Problem

It's tempting to assume AI-assisted defect-detection tools solve a labor shortage by reducing headcount need. That doesn't match how the technology actually works in practice. As covered in more detail on our AI in NDT defect detection page, the industry-consensus role for AI in inspection today is triage — flagging likely-defect regions on PAUT C-scans and digital radiographs so a certified inspector's review time gets prioritized — not autonomous disposition. SNT-TC-1A and ASME Section V Article 1 still require a qualified, certified person to interpret and disposition every result, with an NDT Level III holding final technical authority. If anything, AI-assisted triage that lets existing crews get through more data faster increases the value of every certified technician on staff rather than reducing the need for them — it doesn't remove the qualification requirement or the headcount needed to review flagged data, write procedures, and sign reports.

What Actually Helps

  • Training pipeline investment: The industry's own workforce-development priority, as identified by the American Society for Nondestructive Testing, centers on getting more new entrants into certification programs — school outreach, veterans transition programs, and general visibility of NDT as a viable, well-paying technical career. See Atlantis NDT training programs across Level I, II, and III.
  • Portable, recognized certification: A certification path that's portable between employers (ACCP) rather than locked to a single employer's Written Practice lowers friction for technicians moving where the work and pay are best, which helps the labor market clear faster. See our ASNT certification guide for the SNT-TC-1A vs ACCP comparison.
  • Clear career-path visibility: Salary transparency matters for attracting new entrants into a multi-year certification pathway — see our global NDT salary guide for the actual pay bands by level, method, and region.
  • Reducing the administrative drag on existing technicians: Time NDT Level IIs and IIIs spend on manual certification tracking, procedure version control, and audit-finding remediation is time not spent on billable inspection or mentoring newer technicians. This is a real, unglamorous lever — less about attracting new people and more about not wasting the experienced people already on staff.

What This Means for Employers

The honest takeaway for inspection companies and asset owners: the workforce shortage is a multi-year structural issue that gets addressed through sustained training investment and reducing friction in the certification and career pathway — not through a single software purchase, AI or otherwise. Technology that removes administrative drag on the technicians already on staff, and training programs that shorten the on-ramp for new entrants without cutting corners on the logged-hour and practical-exam requirements that make certification mean something, are the levers that actually move the number.
